sideshows.title: Gear That Made the Sound
sideshows.description: The synths and samplers behind the noise — a journey through machines, not places.

cards.title: ARP 2600
cards.subtitle: The first voice
cards.body: A semi-modular monosynth that gave the earliest records their bright, springy leads. Patch a cable wrong and you got happy accidents — exactly the spirit of a band teaching itself electronics in a Basildon bedroom.

cards.title: E-mu Emulator
cards.subtitle: Sampling changes everything
cards.body: From Construction Time Again onward, the band sampled the real world — anvils, scrap metal, a smashed bottle — and played it back on a keyboard. Industrial sounds became melody. Pop would never sound the same.

cards.title: PPG Wave
cards.subtitle: The cold digital shimmer
cards.body: That glassy, slightly unreal texture across the mid-80s albums is the PPG's wavetable digital synthesis — the sound of the future arriving with a blue glow.

cards.title: Synclavier
cards.subtitle: The expensive monster
cards.body: A fearsomely costly digital workstation that Alan Wilder pushed to its limits for sampling and sound design — a big part of why Black Celebration sounds so vast and precise.

cards.title: Roland TR-808 & friends
cards.subtitle: The pulse underneath
cards.body: Drum machines gave the band their relentless heartbeat. No drummer, no kit — just programmed rhythm, machine-tight, that a hundred thousand people could move to in a stadium.

cards.title: The voice as instrument
cards.subtitle: Sampled, looped, layered
cards.body: By Violator, even Dave's voice and Martin's harmonies were treated as raw material — chopped, layered and folded back into the productions. The most human instrument, run through the machines.

sideshows.title: Sleeves & Symbols
sideshows.description: The artwork and icons that became as recognisable as the songs.

cards.title: The Rose
cards.subtitle: Violator, 1990
cards.body: Anton Corbijn's single red rose against black is one of the most recognised images in pop. Beauty with a thorn — the perfect emblem for an album about desire and control.

cards.title: The Worker
cards.subtitle: Construction Time Again, 1983
cards.body: Brian Griffin's photo of a man swinging a sledgehammer on an Alpine peak framed the band's turn toward industry, politics and the sampled clang of real labour.

cards.title: The Loudhailer
cards.subtitle: Music for the Masses, 1987
cards.body: Bright orange speakers planted in empty landscapes — and on billboards with no band name at all. An ironic title made into an unforgettable, slightly absurd visual campaign.

cards.title: Corbijn's World
cards.subtitle: 1986 onward
cards.body: From Strangelove onward, Anton Corbijn shaped nearly every video, sleeve and stage set — grainy, romantic, dryly funny. The band's entire visual identity is, in large part, his.

cards.title: The Devotional Stage
cards.body: Corbijn's towering screens and stark lighting turned the Devotional tour into a cathedral of sound and image — the look that every arena tour since has chased.
